claims.text: Four principles: autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence and justice.
claims.quote: Four main bioethical principles broadly guided the development of these guidelines: autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice.

claims.text: Autonomy: patients have the right to make their own decisions, and PAs respect them.
claims.quote: Patients have the right to make autonomous decisions and choices, and PAs should respect these decisions and choices.

claims.text: Beneficence: act in the patient's best interest.
claims.quote: Beneficence means that PAs should act in the patient’s best interest.

claims.text: Nonmaleficence: do no harm; impose no unnecessary or unacceptable burden.
claims.quote: Nonmaleficence means to do no harm, to impose no unnecessary or unacceptable burden upon the patient.

claims.text: Justice: patients in similar circumstances should receive similar care.
claims.quote: Justice means that patients in similar circumstances should receive similar care.

claims.text: Adolescents: balance family support with the adolescent's need for confidentiality and emerging autonomy.
claims.quote: In cases of adolescent patients, family support is important but should be balanced with the patient’s need for confidentiality and the PA’s obligation to respect their emerging autonomy.

claims.text: Conflicts of interest: put service to patients before personal material gain and avoid undue influence on clinical judgment.
claims.quote: PAs should place service to patients before personal material gain and should avoid undue influence on their clinical judgment.

claims.text: Disclose; avoid gifts: disclose any actual or potential conflict of interest to patients; accepting gifts, trips or hospitality is discouraged.
claims.quote: PAs should disclose any actual or potential conflict of interest to their patients. Acceptance of gifts, trips, hospitality, or other items is discouraged.

claims.text: Relationships: it is unethical to become sexually involved with patients, and may be unethical with former patients or key third parties (eg, a spouse, parent or surrogate).
claims.quote: It is unethical for PAs to become sexually involved with patients. It also may be unethical for PAs to become sexually involved with former patients or key third parties. Key third parties are individuals who have influence over the patient. These might include spouses or partners, parents, guardians, or surrogates.

claims.text: Impaired colleagues: PAs have an ethical duty to identify and assist impaired colleagues (unable to practice with reasonable skill and safety because of illness, loss of motor skills, or drug or alcohol use), including supervising physicians, and to seek help so they get treatment.
claims.quote: PAs have an ethical responsibility to protect patients and the public by identifying and assisting impaired colleagues. “Impaired” means being unable to practice medicine with reasonable skill and safety because of physical or mental illness, loss of motor skills, or excessive use or abuse of drugs and alcohol. PAs should be able to recognize impairment in physician supervisors, PAs, and other health care providers and should seek assistance from appropriate resources to encourage these individuals to obtain treatment.
